intro.title: A value from another query
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This quest's database is a small music streaming service: `artists`, their `tracks`, the `listeners`, every time a listener `plays` a track, and which artists each listener `follows`. Open **Tables** to see them.

Which tracks are longer than average? You could work out the average first, then type it into a second query. A **subquery** does both at once: a whole query in brackets, used where a value would go.

```
SELECT title, duration_s
FROM tracks
WHERE duration_s > (SELECT AVG(duration_s) FROM tracks);
```

SQLite runs the query in brackets first, gets one number, and uses it in the comparison. Typing the number in yourself would work today, but would be wrong as soon as a track is added; the subquery always uses the current average.

A subquery used as a value must give **one column**. It should also give one row. If it gives no rows, its value is `NULL`. If it gives several, SQLite quietly uses the first one, and most other databases give an error, so make sure it can only give one, for example with an aggregate like `MAX` or with `LIMIT 1`.

A value subquery can go anywhere a value can, including the `SELECT` list. This shows how far each track is from the average:

```
SELECT title,
       duration_s - (SELECT AVG(duration_s) FROM tracks) AS diff
FROM tracks;
```

A good habit: run the subquery on its own in the sandbox first, check its result, then put it in brackets inside the bigger query.

intro.title: IN with a subquery
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A subquery that returns a whole column of values can follow `IN`. The row is kept when its value is somewhere in that list:

```
SELECT title
FROM tracks
WHERE artist_id IN (SELECT id FROM artists WHERE genre = 'jazz');
```

Read it from the inside out: find the ids of the jazz artists, then keep the tracks whose `artist_id` is one of them.

A join could answer the same question, but `IN` has one advantage: it never repeats rows. Joining listeners to their plays repeats a listener once per play; `WHERE id IN (SELECT listener_id FROM plays)` keeps each listener once, however often they played.

`NOT IN` keeps the rows whose value is **not** in the list, such as the tracks nobody has played:

```
SELECT title
FROM tracks
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT track_id FROM plays);
```

One trap: if the list contains a `NULL`, `NOT IN` keeps nothing at all. `3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` isn't true, it's unknown, because the missing value might be 3. When the subquery's column can be `NULL`, add `WHERE column IS NOT NULL` inside it, or use `NOT EXISTS` (coming up in two stages).

Subqueries can be nested: the list itself can come from a query that uses another subquery.

intro.title: Correlated subqueries
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The subqueries so far were complete on their own: you could run them alone. A **correlated** subquery uses a column of the outer query's current row, so it gives a different answer for each row.

Which tracks are longer than their own artist's average?

```
SELECT title, duration_s
FROM tracks t
WHERE duration_s > (
  SELECT AVG(duration_s)
  FROM tracks
  WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id
);
```

For each track `t`, the subquery averages the tracks with the same `artist_id` as `t`. The alias is what makes this work: `t.artist_id` means the outer row's artist, while `artist_id` alone means the inner table's column.

Correlated subqueries are handy in the `SELECT` list too. This counts each listener's plays, and gives 0 to listeners with none, without a `LEFT JOIN`:

```
SELECT name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id) AS plays
FROM listeners l;
```

They also avoid a problem with joins. Joining an artist to both their plays and their followers multiplies the rows (every play times every follower), so the counts come out too big. Two separate correlated subqueries count each thing on its own.

Because a correlated subquery runs once per outer row, it can be slow on big tables. On tables this size, it doesn't matter.

  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tracks t JOIN plays p ON p.track_id = t.id WHERE t.artist_id = a.id) AS plays,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM follows f WHERE f.artist_id = a.id) AS followers
FROM artists a
ORDER BY plays DESC, name;

intro.title: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery returns **at least one row**, whatever is in it. It is almost always correlated: it asks "is there a matching row for this one?"

```
SELECT name
FROM listeners l
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id);
```

For each listener, SQLite looks for a play by them. The `SELECT 1` is a habit: `EXISTS` only cares whether a row exists, not about its columns, so any value will do.

`NOT EXISTS` is the opposite, and the clearest way to find things with no match:

```
SELECT name
FROM listeners l
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id);
```

Unlike `NOT IN`, `NOT EXISTS` has no trap with `NULL` values, because it only asks whether matching rows exist.

The subquery can be as detailed as you need, with joins and several conditions. Listeners who follow an artist but have never played any of their tracks:

```
SELECT l.name AS listener, a.name AS artist
FROM follows f
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = f.listener_id
JOIN artists a ON a.id = f.artist_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  WHERE p.listener_id = f.listener_id
    AND t.artist_id = f.artist_id
);
```

intro.title: Subqueries in FROM
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A query's result is itself a table, so a subquery can go in `FROM`, and the outer query reads from it like any other table. This is how you work with totals of totals.

How many plays does a listener make on average? First count each listener's plays, then average those counts:

```
SELECT AVG(plays) AS average
FROM (
  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays
  GROUP BY listener_id
) AS per_listener;
```

`AVG(COUNT(*))` doesn't work: aggregates can't be nested. The subquery makes one row per listener with their count, and the outer query averages that column.

Give the subquery a name with `AS`. SQLite lets you leave it out, but most databases require it, and you need it to refer to the subquery's columns. Inside, name every calculated column, because those names are the columns of the new table.

A subquery in `FROM` can be joined like a table:

```
SELECT l.name, pl.plays
FROM listeners l
JOIN (
  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays
  GROUP BY listener_id
) AS pl ON pl.listener_id = l.id
ORDER BY pl.plays DESC, l.name;
```

When the same subquery is needed twice, the query gets long and repetitive. The `WITH` stages later in this quest fix that.

intro.title: UNION and UNION ALL
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Joins put tables side by side. `UNION` stacks the results of two queries **on top of each other**, making one longer list:

```
SELECT name FROM artists
UNION
SELECT name FROM listeners;
```

Both queries must give the same number of columns, and the columns are matched by position, not by name. The result takes its column names from the first query.

`UNION` removes duplicate rows from the combined result. `UNION ALL` keeps every row, which is faster and is what you want when repeats matter, such as when you will count them.

A text column added to each part says where each row came from:

```
SELECT 'artist' AS kind, name FROM artists
UNION ALL
SELECT 'listener', name FROM listeners
ORDER BY kind, name;
```

`ORDER BY` goes once, at the very end, and sorts the whole combined result. Here it can only name the result's columns, like `kind` or `name`. To sort by a calculation, put the whole `UNION` in a subquery in `FROM` and sort the outer query.

For one table, `WHERE a OR b` usually does the same as a `UNION` of two queries. `UNION` is what you need when the rows come from **different tables**.

intro.title: INTERSECT and EXCEPT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Two more set operators work like `UNION`, with two queries that have the same number of columns:

`INTERSECT` keeps the rows that appear in **both** results. `EXCEPT` keeps the rows of the first result that do **not** appear in the second. Like `UNION`, both remove duplicates.

Countries with listeners but no artists:

```
SELECT country FROM listeners
EXCEPT
SELECT country FROM artists;
```

They compare whole rows, which makes them neat for pairs. Each (listener, artist) pair that is followed but has never been played:

```
SELECT listener_id, artist_id FROM follows
EXCEPT
SELECT p.listener_id, t.artist_id
FROM plays p
JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id;
```

With `EXCEPT`, the order matters: `A EXCEPT B` and `B EXCEPT A` are different questions. With `INTERSECT` it doesn't.

The result has only the columns you compared. To show names, put the set query in a subquery (in `FROM` or after `IN`) and join or filter from there. As with `UNION`, `ORDER BY` goes once, after the last part.

intro.title: WITH: naming a subquery
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`WITH` gives a subquery a name **before** the main query, which can then use it like a table. Such a named subquery is called a **common table expression**, or CTE.

```
WITH per_listener AS (
  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays
  GROUP BY listener_id
)
SELECT l.name, pl.plays
FROM per_listener pl
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = pl.listener_id
WHERE pl.plays > (SELECT AVG(plays) FROM per_listener)
ORDER BY pl.plays DESC, l.name;
```

Compare it with the last stage, where the counts had to be written twice. Here they are written once and used twice: in `FROM` and inside the subquery for the average.

A query with `WITH` reads from top to bottom: first the steps, then the answer. That makes long queries much easier to follow, and to check: you can test the CTE by itself by putting a plain `SELECT * FROM per_listener;` after it.

The CTE only exists while its query runs; it doesn't create a table. Inside it, name every calculated column with `AS`, or list the names after the CTE's name: `WITH genre_plays(genre, plays) AS (…)`.

GROUP BY plan
ORDER BY plan;

intro.title: Several CTEs
intro.bodyMarkdown:
One `WITH` can hold several CTEs, separated by commas. Write `WITH` only once:

```
WITH artist_plays AS (
  SELECT t.artist_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  GROUP BY t.artist_id
),
artist_followers AS (
  SELECT artist_id, COUNT(*) AS followers
  FROM follows
  GROUP BY artist_id
)
SELECT a.name,
       COALESCE(ap.plays, 0) AS plays,
       COALESCE(af.followers, 0) AS followers
FROM artists a
LEFT JOIN artist_plays ap ON ap.artist_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN artist_followers af ON af.artist_id = a.id;
```

Each CTE counts one thing, so joining them gives one row per artist and the counts can't multiply. `LEFT JOIN` and `COALESCE` keep the artists with nothing to count.

A later CTE can use an earlier one, so a long question becomes a chain of small steps, each easy to check on its own:

```
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT * FROM plays WHERE played_on >= '2026-10-10'
),
recent_listeners AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT listener_id FROM recent
)
SELECT name
FROM listeners
WHERE id IN (SELECT listener_id FROM recent_listeners);
```

A forgotten comma between two CTEs is the most usual error here: SQLite then reports a **syntax error** near the second name.

challenges.solution:
WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT SUBSTR(released, 1, 4) AS year, COUNT(*) AS releases
  FROM tracks
  GROUP BY year
),
yearly_plays AS (
  SELECT SUBSTR(t.released, 1, 4) AS year, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  GROUP BY year

challenges.solution:

  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays FROM plays
  WHERE played_on LIKE '2026-09%'
  GROUP BY listener_id
),
oct AS (
  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays FROM plays
  WHERE played_on LIKE '2026-10%'
  GROUP BY listener_id
)
SELECT l.name,
       COALESCE(s.plays, 0) AS september,
       COALESCE(o.plays, 0) AS october,
       COALESCE(o.plays, 0) - COALESCE(s.plays, 0) AS change
FROM listeners l
LEFT JOIN sept s ON s.listener_id = l.id

ORDER BY change, l.name;

challenges.title: Expert: Loyal and silent followers
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each followed artist, show `name`, the followers who have played them (`loyal`) and the followers who never have (`silent`). In name order.
challenges.hint: CTE 1: distinct (listener_id, artist_id) pairs from plays and tracks. CTE 2: follows LEFT JOIN those pairs, with `CASE WHEN pairs.listener_id IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS played`. Then sum per artist.
challenges.solution:
WITH played_pairs AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT p.listener_id, t.artist_id
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
),
marked AS (
  SELECT f.artist_id,
         CASE WHEN pp.listener_id IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS played
  FROM follows f
  LEFT JOIN played_pairs pp
    ON pp.listener_id = f.listener_id AND pp.artist_id = f.artist_id
)
SELECT a.name, SUM(m.played) AS loyal, COUNT(*) - SUM(m.played) AS silent
FROM marked m
JOIN artists a ON a.id = m.artist_id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.name;

intro.title: The top in each group
intro.bodyMarkdown:
"Each artist's longest track" sounds like a `GROUP BY`, but `GROUP BY artist_id` with `MAX(duration_s)` only gives the length, not the title. You need the whole **row** that holds the top value.

A correlated subquery finds it: keep each track whose length equals the longest length of its own artist.

```
SELECT t.title, t.duration_s
FROM tracks t
WHERE t.duration_s = (
  SELECT MAX(duration_s) FROM tracks WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id
);
```

If two rows tie for the top, both are kept. Sometimes that is right. When you need exactly one row per group, add a rule that breaks ties: let the subquery pick one **id**, sorted by your rule, with `LIMIT 1`:

```
SELECT t.title
FROM tracks t
WHERE t.id = (
  SELECT t2.id FROM tracks t2
  WHERE t2.artist_id = t.artist_id
  ORDER BY t2.duration_s DESC, t2.id
  LIMIT 1
);
```

When the value you rank by is itself a total, like plays per track, work it out in a CTE first, then pick the top rows from the CTE in the same way.

The window functions quest shows a shorter way to do all this, with `ROW_NUMBER()` and `RANK()`. The subquery way works in every database, and helps you see what those functions do.

challenges.title: Easy: Longest per artist
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each artist's name (`artist`) with the `title` and `duration_s` of their longest track. In artist order.
challenges.hint: Join tracks to artists, and keep `t.duration_s = (SELECT MAX(duration_s) FROM tracks WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT a.name AS artist, t.title, t.duration_s
FROM tracks t
JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
WHERE t.duration_s = (
  SELECT MAX(duration_s) FROM tracks WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id
)
ORDER BY artist;

challenges.title: Easy: Newest per artist
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each artist's name (`artist`) with the `title` and `released` date of their newest track (all of them if several came out that day). Sort by artist, then title.
challenges.hint: `t.released = (SELECT MAX(released) FROM tracks WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT a.name AS artist, t.title, t.released
FROM tracks t
JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
WHERE t.released = (
  SELECT MAX(released) FROM tracks WHERE artist_id = t.artist_id
)
ORDER BY artist, t.title;

challenges.title: Easy: First to join
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each `plan`, show the `name` and `joined` date of the listener who joined first. In plan order.
challenges.hint: `WHERE joined = (SELECT MIN(joined) FROM listeners l2 WHERE l2.plan = l.plan)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT plan, name, joined
FROM listeners l
WHERE joined = (SELECT MIN(joined) FROM listeners l2 WHERE l2.plan = l.plan)
ORDER BY plan;

challenges.title: Medium: Latest play
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each listener who played, show their `name`, the date of their latest play (`played_on`) and the `title` of the track they played then. In name order.
challenges.hint: Join plays to listeners and tracks, and keep `p.played_on = (SELECT MAX(played_on) FROM plays WHERE listener_id = p.listener_id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT l.name, p.played_on, t.title
FROM plays p
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = p.listener_id
JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
WHERE p.played_on = (
  SELECT MAX(played_on) FROM plays WHERE listener_id = p.listener_id
)
ORDER BY l.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Hits, with ties
challenges.promptMarkdown: For every artist, show their name (`artist`), and the `title` and `plays` of their most played track. Count plays of all tracks (so unplayed tracks have 0). Show all tracks that tie. Sort by artist, then title.
challenges.hint: A CTE `tp` of (artist_id, title, plays) with a LEFT JOIN to plays, then `WHERE plays = (SELECT MAX(plays) FROM tp AS x WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH tp AS (
  SELECT t.artist_id, t.title, COUNT(p.id) AS plays
  FROM tracks t
  LEFT JOIN plays p ON p.track_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.id, t.artist_id, t.title
)
SELECT a.name AS artist, tp.title, tp.plays
FROM tp
JOIN artists a ON a.id = tp.artist_id
WHERE tp.plays = (SELECT MAX(plays) FROM tp AS x WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id)
ORDER BY artist, tp.title;

challenges.title: Hard: One hit each
challenges.promptMarkdown: Now exactly one track per artist: show `artist`, `title` and `plays` of each artist's most played track. If tracks tie, take the one released first, then the lower id. In artist order.
challenges.hint: In the CTE keep `t.id` and `t.released` too, then `WHERE tp.id = (SELECT x.id FROM tp AS x WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id ORDER BY x.plays DESC, x.released, x.id LIMIT 1)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH tp AS (
  SELECT t.id, t.artist_id, t.title, t.released, COUNT(p.id) AS plays
  FROM tracks t
  LEFT JOIN plays p ON p.track_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.id, t.artist_id, t.title, t.released
)
SELECT a.name AS artist, tp.title, tp.plays
FROM tp
JOIN artists a ON a.id = tp.artist_id
WHERE tp.id = (
  SELECT x.id FROM tp AS x
  WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id
  ORDER BY x.plays DESC, x.released, x.id
  LIMIT 1
)
ORDER BY artist;

challenges.title: Hard: Favourite artists
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each listener who played, show their `name`, their favourite artist (most plays, called `artist`) and those `plays`. If artists tie, take the one whose name comes first alphabetically. In name order.
challenges.hint: A CTE of (listener_id, artist_id, artist name, plays), then keep the row whose artist_id is the first one from `ORDER BY plays DESC, artist_name LIMIT 1` for that listener.
challenges.solution:
WITH la AS (
  SELECT p.listener_id, a.id AS artist_id, a.name AS artist, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
  GROUP BY p.listener_id, a.id, a.name
)
SELECT l.name, la.artist, la.plays
FROM la
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = la.listener_id
WHERE la.artist_id = (
  SELECT x.artist_id FROM la AS x
  WHERE x.listener_id = la.listener_id
  ORDER BY x.plays DESC, x.artist
  LIMIT 1
)
ORDER BY l.name;

challenges.title: Expert: Top two per artist
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each artist's two most played tracks: `artist`, `title` and `plays` (unplayed tracks count as 0, so an artist with one track shows one row). Ties are broken by title. Sort by artist, then most plays, then title.
challenges.hint: From a CTE of plays per track, keep a track when fewer than 2 tracks of the same artist rank above it: `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tp AS x WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id AND (x.plays > tp.plays OR (x.plays = tp.plays AND x.title < tp.title))) < 2`.
challenges.solution:
WITH tp AS (
  SELECT t.artist_id, t.title, COUNT(p.id) AS plays
  FROM tracks t
  LEFT JOIN plays p ON p.track_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.id, t.artist_id, t.title
)
SELECT a.name AS artist, tp.title, tp.plays
FROM tp
JOIN artists a ON a.id = tp.artist_id
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tp AS x
  WHERE x.artist_id = tp.artist_id
    AND (x.plays > tp.plays OR (x.plays = tp.plays AND x.title < tp.title))
) < 2
ORDER BY artist, tp.plays DESC, tp.title;

challenges.title: Expert: Most followed per genre
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each `genre`, show the most followed artist (`artist`) and their `followers`. Show every artist that ties. Sort by genre, then artist.
challenges.hint: A CTE of (genre, artist, followers) with a correlated subquery or join for the counts, then keep the rows whose followers equal the genre's maximum.
challenges.solution:
WITH af AS (
  SELECT a.genre, a.name AS artist,
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM follows f WHERE f.artist_id = a.id) AS followers
  FROM artists a
)
SELECT genre, artist, followers
FROM af
WHERE followers = (SELECT MAX(followers) FROM af AS x WHERE x.genre = af.genre)
ORDER BY genre, artist;

challenges.title: Easy: Long listens
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` and artist name (`artist`) of every track longer than the average track. In title order.
challenges.hint: Join tracks to artists, `WHERE t.duration_s > (SELECT AVG(duration_s) FROM tracks) ORDER BY t.title`.

SELECT t.title, a.name AS artist
FROM tracks t
JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id

challenges.title: Easy: Top five
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the five most played tracks: `title` and `plays`. Most first; equal plays in title order.
challenges.hint: Group plays by track, join the titles, `ORDER BY plays DESC, t.title LIMIT 5`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT t.title, COUNT(*) AS plays
FROM plays p
JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
GROUP BY t.id, t.title
ORDER BY plays DESC, t.title
LIMIT 5;

challenges.hint: `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id) AS plays … WHERE released >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY released DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT title, released,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id) AS plays
FROM tracks t
WHERE released >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY released DESC;

challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` and artist name (`artist`) of every track that has never been played.
challenges.hint: Join tracks to artists, `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id)`.

SELECT t.title, a.name AS artist
FROM tracks t
JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id);

challenges.title: Hard: Artist chart
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the top three artists by plays: `name`, `plays` and `followers`. Use one CTE per count. Most plays first; ties in name order.
challenges.hint: CTEs artist_plays and artist_followers, joined to artists, `ORDER BY plays DESC, a.name LIMIT 3`.
challenges.solution:
WITH artist_plays AS (
  SELECT t.artist_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  GROUP BY t.artist_id
),
artist_followers AS (
  SELECT artist_id, COUNT(*) AS followers
  FROM follows
  GROUP BY artist_id
)
SELECT a.name, ap.plays, COALESCE(af.followers, 0) AS followers
FROM artists a
JOIN artist_plays ap ON ap.artist_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN artist_followers af ON af.artist_id = a.id
ORDER BY ap.plays DESC, a.name
LIMIT 3;

FROM gt

intro.title: Medium side quest: Listener insights
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The product team wants to understand the listeners: who never started, who listens most, who follows artists without listening to them, and what each listener likes best.

Listeners without plays should appear wherever the question is about every listener.

challenges.title: Easy: Never started
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name`, `plan` and `joined` date of every listener with no plays, earliest joined first.
challenges.hint: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id) ORDER BY joined`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, plan, joined
FROM listeners l
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id)
ORDER BY joined;

challenges.title: Medium: Keen listeners
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name`, `plan` and `plays` of the listeners with more plays than the average listener who played. Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: A CTE of plays per listener, joined to listeners, `WHERE plays > (SELECT AVG(plays) FROM cte)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH per_listener AS (
  SELECT listener_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays
  GROUP BY listener_id
)
SELECT l.name, l.plan, pl.plays
FROM per_listener pl
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = pl.listener_id
WHERE pl.plays > (SELECT AVG(plays) FROM per_listener)
ORDER BY pl.plays DESC, l.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Follows without listening
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every listener's `name` and how many of the artists they follow they have never played (`unplayed_follows`), including 0. In name order.
challenges.hint: A correlated count of follows f for this listener `WHERE NOT EXISTS` a play by them of a track by f.artist_id.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name,
  (SELECT COUNT(*)
   FROM follows f
   WHERE f.listener_id = l.id
     AND NOT EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM plays p
       JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
       WHERE p.listener_id = l.id AND t.artist_id = f.artist_id
     )
  ) AS unplayed_follows
FROM listeners l
ORDER BY name;

challenges.title: Medium: No electronic yet
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name` of every premium listener who has never played an `electronic` track.
challenges.hint: `WHERE plan = 'premium' AND id NOT IN (listener ids of plays of electronic tracks)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name
FROM listeners
WHERE plan = 'premium'
  AND id NOT IN (
    SELECT p.listener_id
    FROM plays p
    JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
    JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
    WHERE a.genre = 'electronic'
  );

challenges.title: Hard: Favourite genre
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each listener who played, show `name`, their favourite `genre` (most plays; ties go to the genre first in alphabetical order) and those `plays`. In name order.
challenges.hint: A CTE of (listener_id, genre, plays), then keep the row whose genre is the first from `ORDER BY plays DESC, genre LIMIT 1` for that listener.
challenges.solution:
WITH lg AS (
  SELECT p.listener_id, a.genre, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
  GROUP BY p.listener_id, a.genre
)
SELECT l.name, lg.genre, lg.plays
FROM lg
JOIN listeners l ON l.id = lg.listener_id
WHERE lg.genre = (
  SELECT x.genre FROM lg AS x
  WHERE x.listener_id = lg.listener_id
  ORDER BY x.plays DESC, x.genre
  LIMIT 1
)
ORDER BY l.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Listener cards
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one card per listener: `name`, `plan`, `plays`, number of different artists played (`artists`) and date of the last play (`last_played`, NULL if none). Most plays first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Three correlated subqueries in the SELECT list: COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT t.artist_id) and MAX(played_on), each for this listener.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, plan,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id) AS plays,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT t.artist_id) FROM plays p JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id WHERE p.listener_id = l.id) AS artists,
  (SELECT MAX(played_on) FROM plays p WHERE p.listener_id = l.id) AS last_played
FROM listeners l
ORDER BY plays DESC, name;

intro.title: Hard side quest: Catalogue review
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The label is reviewing its catalogue. It wants a profile of each artist, the tracks that reach every kind of listener, the gaps in what people have discovered, and how well follows turn into listening.

Use whichever tools fit: subqueries, EXISTS, set operators and CTEs. Build each answer step by step in the sandbox.

challenges.title: Medium: Artist profiles
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each artist, show `name`, number of tracks (`tracks`), average length rounded to 1 decimal (`average_s`) and the title of their longest track (`longest`; the lowest id if two tie). In name order.
challenges.hint: Group tracks by artist for the counts, and for the title use a correlated subquery: `(SELECT title FROM tracks t2 WHERE t2.artist_id = a.id ORDER BY duration_s DESC, id LIMIT 1)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS tracks, ROUND(AVG(t.duration_s), 1) AS average_s,
  (SELECT t2.title FROM tracks t2 WHERE t2.artist_id = a.id ORDER BY t2.duration_s DESC, t2.id LIMIT 1) AS longest
FROM artists a
JOIN tracks t ON t.artist_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Every kind of listener
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` of every track played by at least one free listener and at least one premium listener. In title order.
challenges.hint: `WHERE id IN (track ids played by free listeners INTERSECT track ids played by premium listeners)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT title
FROM tracks
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT p.track_id FROM plays p JOIN listeners l ON l.id = p.listener_id WHERE l.plan = 'free'
  INTERSECT
  SELECT p.track_id FROM plays p JOIN listeners l ON l.id = p.listener_id WHERE l.plan = 'premium'
)
ORDER BY title;

challenges.title: Hard: Complete or with gaps
challenges.promptMarkdown: Label every artist: `complete` if all their tracks have been played, `gaps` otherwise. Show `name` and `status`, built as a `UNION ALL` of two queries, in name order.
challenges.hint: One query with NOT EXISTS an unplayed track (`'complete' AS status`), the other with EXISTS an unplayed track (`'gaps'`).
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, 'complete' AS status
FROM artists a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM tracks t
  WHERE t.artist_id = a.id
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id)
)
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'gaps'
FROM artists a
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM tracks t
  WHERE t.artist_id = a.id
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plays p WHERE p.track_id = t.id)
)
ORDER BY name;

challenges.title: Hard: Share of listening
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every artist's `name`, `plays` (0 if none) and share of all plays (`percent`, 1 decimal). Most plays first, then by name.
challenges.hint: A CTE of plays per artist, LEFT JOINed to artists; `ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(ap.plays, 0) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays), 1)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH artist_plays AS (
  SELECT t.artist_id, COUNT(*) AS plays
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
  GROUP BY t.artist_id
)
SELECT a.name,
       COALESCE(ap.plays, 0) AS plays,
       ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(ap.plays, 0) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plays), 1) AS percent
FROM artists a
LEFT JOIN artist_plays ap ON ap.artist_id = a.id
ORDER BY plays DESC, a.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Top two per genre
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each genre's two most played tracks (counting plays of all tracks, so unplayed tracks count as 0): `genre`, `title`, `plays`. Ties are broken by title. Sort by genre, then most plays, then title.
challenges.hint: A CTE of (genre, title, plays) with a LEFT JOIN to plays, then keep the rows with fewer than 2 better rows in the same genre.
challenges.solution:
WITH gt AS (
  SELECT a.genre, t.title, COUNT(p.id) AS plays
  FROM tracks t
  JOIN artists a ON a.id = t.artist_id
  LEFT JOIN plays p ON p.track_id = t.id
  GROUP BY a.genre, t.id, t.title
)
SELECT genre, title, plays
FROM gt
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gt AS x
  WHERE x.genre = gt.genre
    AND (x.plays > gt.plays OR (x.plays = gt.plays AND x.title < gt.title))
) < 2
ORDER BY genre, plays DESC, title;

challenges.title: Hard: From follow to play
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each followed artist, show `name`, `followers`, the followers who have played them (`listening`) and that as a percentage of followers (`percent`, 1 decimal). Highest percentage first, then by name.
challenges.hint: For each follow, test with EXISTS whether that listener played that artist (1 or 0) in a CTE, then group by artist.
challenges.solution:
WITH marked AS (
  SELECT f.artist_id,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM plays p
      JOIN tracks t ON t.id = p.track_id
      WHERE p.listener_id = f.listener_id AND t.artist_id = f.artist_id
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS played
  FROM follows f
)
SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS followers, SUM(m.played) AS listening,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(m.played) / COUNT(*), 1) AS percent
FROM marked m
JOIN artists a ON a.id = m.artist_id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY percent DESC, a.name;
